section_1.title: The Problem: How Fast is the Cheetah Moving?
section_1.content: Introduce the limitation of average speed. Calculus begins when we try to find the instantaneous speed of an object (like a sprinting cheetah) at an exact point in time, where distance and time change become 'almost' zero.
section_1.example: A cheetah runs 100 meters in 5 seconds. Average speed is easy (20 m/s), but how fast is it running at exactly the 2-second mark?

section_2.title: The Bridge: The Concept of Limits
section_2.content: Explain 'Limits' as the prerequisite. We zoom into a graph, getting closer and closer to a point without ever needing to land exactly on it. This visual 'zooming in' allows us to define the tangent slope.
section_2.example: Animation: A line on a graph getting closer to a curve until the straight line and the curve appear identical at a microscopic level.

section_3.title: Differentiation: Measuring Change
section_3.content: Define the derivative as the 'slope of the curve.' If the y-axis is distance and the x-axis is time, the derivative is the speedometer of the cheetah. It tells us how the function is changing at any single instant.
section_3.example: Visual: A speedometer needle on the cheetah's dashboard that changes value fluidly as the cheetah accelerates.

section_4.title: Integration: Accumulating the Whole
section_4.content: Introduce Integration as the reverse process. If we know the speed at every moment, how do we find the total distance covered? We break the area under a curve into infinite tiny rectangles and sum them up.
section_4.example: Visual: A complex, wavy shape on a screen being filled by an infinite number of razor-thin vertical bars that perfectly sum up to the total area.

section_5.title: The Fundamental Connection
section_5.content: Conclude by showing that Differentiation (slicing into pieces) and Integration (gluing pieces together) are inverse operations—the 'Fundamental Theorem of Calculus'.
section_5.example: The cheetah analogy: Differentiation turns 'total distance' into 'instant speed'; Integration turns 'instant speed' back into 'total distance'.

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject
